claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles as a function of particle size.
FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles exhibit size-dependent thermal responses.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have greater thermal stability than smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The initial material consists of synthesized FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles spanning a range of sizes at ambient conditions.
Controlled temperature ramps can be applied to these nanoparticles in atomistic MD simulations using realistic interatomic potentials.
The simulations can use NPT or NVT ensembles over temperatures near the thermal-stability threshold.
Atomic reordering and diffusion in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are modulated by the surface-to-volume ratio.
Larger nanoparticles have a lower surface-to-volume ratio than smaller nanoparticles.
Surface atoms are relatively high-energy atoms.
A lower surface-to-volume ratio reduces the relative influence of high-energy surface atoms.
Reducing the influence of surface atoms delays surface-induced structural rearrangement or disorder during heating.
Delayed structural rearrangement or disorder produces a higher thermal-stability threshold in larger nanoparticles.
The onset temperature for significant atomic diffusion or phase transformation increases with FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle size.
Randomized atomic distributions are representative initial configurations for the stated HEA composition.
Surface phenomena dominate the thermal behavior over the nanoscale particle-size range considered.
The predicted quantitative size–stability relationship is sensitive to multielement interactions, simulation parameters, and the selected interatomic potential.
Marked increases in diffusion or structural disorder can operationally identify the onset of thermal instability.
